AWS DevOps Agent adds upcoming chat capabilities

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (154 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS DevOps Agent now extends its chat capabilities across MCP clients like Kiro and Claude Code, as well as Slack and Microsoft Teams channels.
  • Sources indicate that this launch also adds auto-creation of per-incident Slack code channels and bi-directional chat within Microsoft Teams.
  • See all the latest AWS DevOps Agent features on the release history page.

AWS DevOps Agent now extends its chat capabilities across MCP clients like Kiro and Claude Code, as well as Slack and Microsoft Teams channels. With Model Context Protocol (MCP) support, AWS DevOps Agent can now take directed chat actions including support for GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, ServiceNow, and PagerDuty MCP tools, giving developers and operations teams powerful workflow automation directly from their preferred chat interface.

Sources indicate that this launch also adds auto-creation of per-incident Slack code channels and bi-directional chat within Microsoft Teams. AWS DevOps Agent has access to a compute sandbox that it can use to execute scripts and access the network to work more efficiently, and people can now rename and archive chats across all supported platforms.

See all the latest AWS DevOps Agent features on the release history page. For the list of AWS Regions where AWS DevOps Agent is available, see the supported Regions table.

AWS DevOps Agent adds community and partner tools repository

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (202 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS DevOps Agent now gives you ways to share and leverage skills, MCP servers, connectors, and custom agents that enhance the capabilities of your AWS DevOps Agent instances.
  • According to recent reports, the AWS DevOps Agent Tools open source repository is a centralized, AWS-curated collection of tools that extend AWS DevOps Agent capabilities.
  • To get started, browse the skills and connector catalogs from within your AWS DevOps Agent instance, or add and share your own tools by creating a PR within the AWS DevOps Agent Tools repository.

AWS DevOps Agent now gives you ways to share and leverage skills, MCP servers, connectors, and custom agents that enhance the capabilities of your AWS DevOps Agent instances.

According to recent reports, the AWS DevOps Agent Tools open source repository is a centralized, AWS-curated collection of tools that extend AWS DevOps Agent capabilities. Customers can import ready-to-use, quality-controlled tools directly into their DevOps Agent configurations to improve investigation quality and expand operational context. A growing community of AWS DevOps Agent users and partners, and AWS service and support teams, have contributed a growing collection of tools to the community, including several partner-managed connectors that simplify connecting AWS DevOps Agent to third party MCP servers. Partners providing connectors include: Bluebox, Bronto, Celonis, Clickhouse Observability, Coralogix, Cribl, Elastic, Halo, Honeycomb, LaunchDarkly, Neo4j, Sumo Logic, and Wiz.

To get started, browse the skills and connector catalogs from within your AWS DevOps Agent instance, or add and share your own tools by creating a PR within the AWS DevOps Agent Tools repository.

See all the latest AWS DevOps Agent features on the release history page. For the list of AWS Regions where AWS DevOps Agent is available, see the supported Regions table.

Breaking: Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (616 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package).
  • It has been revealed that the torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

It has been revealed that the torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

Recent findings suggest that the Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

It has been revealed that to look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

According to recent reports, at the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We initiative to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

It has been revealed that select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:.

No need for torchrun: the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

Sources indicate that A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:.

In a recent development, each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

Recent findings suggest that at the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space highlights comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:.

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

Almost $1bn raised in FinTech deals in strong week for investment

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1969 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fintech

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Across the 17 deals reported on by FinTech Global this week, there was a total of $991m raised – showcasing a continuous strength in firms securing investment.
  • This was up on last week, where total of $602m was raised across 14 FinTech deals, a small increase on the previous week where $454.4m was raised across 12 deals.
  • Two of the top deals this week came from Bulgarian PayTech firm Payhawk and Model ML, a personal AI platform for financial and professional services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Across the 17 deals reported on by FinTech Global this week, there was a total of $991m raised – showcasing a continuous strength in firms securing investment.

This was up on last week, where total of $602m was raised across 14 FinTech deals, a small increase on the previous week where $454.4m was raised across 12 deals.

Two of the top deals this week came from Bulgarian PayTech firm Payhawk and Model ML, a personal AI platform for financial and professional services.

In a recent development, geographically, the US secured the most deals this week with 8 in total. Trailing in second was Canada with three, whilst Israel, Egypt, Spain, Georgia, the UK and Bulgaria pulled in one.

In a recent development, market-wise, financial infrastructure firms made up the majority of this week’s deals with four. In joint second were WealthTech and CyberTech firms on three, PayTech, InsurTech and Blockchain firms secured two.

In a recent development, this week, research from FinTech Global showcased findings of a powerful performance for Global FinTech in this year’s third quarter. The Global FinTech market attracted $27.5bn across 1,275 deals in Q3 2026. Funding climbed 35% from $20.3bn in Q3 2025 but fell 11% from $30.9bn in Q2 2026.

Deal volume fell 2% from 1,306 transactions in Q3 2025 and rose 5% from 1,220 in Q2 2026.

Payhawk raises $280m to build AI-era Finance OS.

Payhawk, the Sofia-founded spend management and finance platform, has closed a $280m Series C round led by Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives. The deal values the company at $2bn.

According to recent reports, the raise takes Payhawk’s total funding past $515m. Every existing backer returned for the round, among them QED, Greenoaks, Lightspeed, Hedosophia and Bek Ventures.

They were joined by first-time investors Galdana Ventures, Cogito Capital, Inveready and Invus, as well as European founders Tomas Okmanas and Didac Lee.

Model ML bags $250m to give every banker an AI agent.

Model ML, a London-based personal AI platform for financial and professional services, has secured $250m in a Series B round that values the organization at $1.5bn.

General Atlantic and QED Investors co-led the investment. Evolution Equity Partners, Airtree, Forestay Capital, Y Combinator, FT Partners, Latitude, Inception Fund and 13Books Capital also took part. The deal lifts the total capital raised by Model ML to $350m.

The raise comes after a period of rapid expansion. Over the third quarter of 2026, annual recurring revenue at the firm increased twelvefold compared with the same period a year earlier, while daily active users rose 26-fold.

Blue J lands $176m to put AI agents on tax desks.

Blue J, a tax research and advisory platform, has secured $176m in a Series E round that values the business at above $700m, as it moves beyond answering tax questions to handing the actual workload over to AI agents.

JMI Equity, a growth equity investor, led the raise. Existing backers Oak HC/FT and Sapphire Ventures returned for the round, joined by Intrepid Growth Partners. The valuation also exceeds C$1bn. As part of the deal, JMI Equity principal Jack Duane will take a seat on the Blue J board.

The firm plans to put the capital behind Workflows, its agentic AI product for tax practitioners, and to push further into the United Kingdom and other international markets.

Corma hits $1bn valuation with $125m Series A.

Corma, an AI research lab building foundation models for defensive cybersecurity, has secured $125m in Series A funding at a $1bn valuation, only three months after revealing its seed round.

NEA led the investment, with participation from returning backers Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures and Coatue. The latest raise takes the company’s total funding to $185m.

Corma’s $60m seed round, led by Sequoia, was unveiled in August.

TBC Georgia secures $51m as ADB and IFC back trade finance.

TBC Georgia, a leading Georgian financial institution and member of the London-listed TBC Bank Group, has raised $51m from international commercial banks to widen the availability of trade finance for businesses across Georgia.

The capital comes with guarantee backing from the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the International Finance Corporation (IFC).

Sources indicate that it is channelled through two established schemes: the ADB’s Trade and Supply Chain Finance Program and the IFC’s Global Trade Finance Program. Because both institutions stand behind the facility, commercial lenders can extend capital to the Georgian market with added assurance.

Codex lands $30m Series A to scale stablecoin FX.

Codex, a platform that provides foreign exchange infrastructure for stablecoins and fiat currencies, has secured $30m in Series A funding to expand its cross-border payments business.

Pantera headed the investment, which also drew backing from Dragonfly, Coinbase Ventures, Tenet, Reciprocal, Fin Capital, LeadBlock and additional investors. The deal puts the firm’s post-money valuation at $130m.

Both Dragonfly and Coinbase Ventures have backed Codex before, having taken part in its seed round.

Arva AI lands $20m Series A for AI banking agents.

Arva AI, a company that deploys AI agents to make critical banking decisions, has secured $20m in Series A funding as it looks to push its accuracy-focused technology deeper into the bank back office.

According to the company, most back-office decisions at banks are still made manually, but this has begun to shift. Over the past year, Arva’s customers started entrusting important decisions to its agents, with staff setting policies and monitoring outcomes.

During that period the firm rolled out its technology at scale with banks and FinTechs, among them a top-10 US bank, a payments institution listed on the S&P 500 and the global FinTech Wise.

StepSecurity bags $20m as supply chain attacks escalate.

Elephant led the round, and existing backers Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital and SaaS Ventures also took part. Together with a $3m seed round raised earlier, the deal lifts StepSecurity’s total funding to $23m.

The organization plans to use the money to speed up development and wider rollout of its platform, which is designed to stop malicious packages at every checkpoint of the agentic software pipeline.

Vero Security raises $11m as AI security jobs go unstaffed.

Vero Security, a start-up developing a platform for AI Security Engineering, has closed an $11m seed round as large enterprises struggle to staff a responsibility that most still treat as a side duty.

TLV Partners led the investment, joined by GTM Capital, Maple Capital and a group of angel backers. Vero was established in 2025 and has already signed several Fortune 500 businesses as customers.

Alongside the raise, it is introducing AISecurityEngineering.org, an open community and knowledge hub offering practical field guides, workshops and the ASE credential track for practitioners shaping this latest specialism.

Roadzen raises $10m for India arm at $300m valuation.

Roadzen, which applies AI to insurance and mobility, has secured roughly $10m (₹94 crore) for its Indian subsidiary, Roadzen AI Limited, which is now valued at about $300m post-money on a stand-alone basis.

According to recent reports, the round is being raised entirely as common equity. It carries no warrants or preferred rights, and the upcoming shares rank equally with those held by the existing shareholder, Roadzen.

In a recent development, because the capital goes into the subsidiary, shareholders in the Nasdaq-listed parent will not be diluted. Family offices and capital markets investors anchored the deal. Several of them had backed the organization’s earlier India subsidiary round and raised their commitments this time.

Valeria bags €5.5m seed to scale AI payroll engine.

Valeria, a Barcelona-headquartered payroll and workforce management platform built on artificial intelligence, has secured €5.5m in seed funding to expand its technology for businesses that see frequent staff changes.

The round was led by BlackFin, with returning backers VentureFriends and Fortino also participating. GoHub Ventures came on board as a new investor in the company.

The seed raise follows a €1.7m pre-seed round completed in February 2026, meaning Valeria has secured over €7m in total during 2026.

WealthTech finny raises Rs 5.3 Cr angel round.

finny, a WealthTech start-up offering personalised financial advice, has reportedly secured Rs 5.3 Cr (around $560,000) through an angel round, according to a report from BW Disrupt.

A group of high-profile backers joined the round. Among them were Ramanathan RV, who founded both Hyperface and Juspay, and Anil Goel, who serves as Global CTO at Nielsen. Uday Sodhi, previously an executive at Sony Pictures, also took part, as did Aditya Pittie, MD and CEO of Pittie Group. Angel syndicate Zorvian LLP was among the other participants.

The company intends to split the new money across three priorities. A portion will go towards R&D, with an emphasis on building out its AI-driven products.

Pretxt raises $5m to keep AI agents within the rules.

Pretxt, a newly debuted enterprise AI tech giant focused on runtime oversight of AI agents, has stepped out of stealth mode with $5m in seed capital to build out a technology category it calls AI Supervision.

In a recent development, deciens Capital, Howdy Partners, Service Provider Capital and NSV Wolf Capital backed the round. Pretxt plans to use the capital to bring its supervision layer to enterprises that want AI agents to handle higher-stakes work without drifting from approved procedures.

AI agents no longer simply produce text. They now speak with customers, connect to other systems, handle transactions and run business processes. According to Pretxt, these agents do not always behave as instructed.

Verlo raises $4.5m to cut admin work for wealth firms.

Verlo, a provider of an AI operating system built for wealth management firms, has secured $4.5m CAD in seed funding to help Registered Investment Advisors (RIAs) cut back on time-consuming administrative tasks.

Staircase Ventures led the investment, while Pelorus VC came back to back the organization again. They were joined by several angel investors, among them founders and senior executives from Verafin, the Newfoundland financial crime software business that Nasdaq bought in 2020 for $2.7bn.

Global Kiwi Labs raises $4m for TheHUB.

Global Kiwi Labs, the developer behind digital asset colocation network TheHUB, has closed a $4m seed round as it looks to bring the equal-access trading architecture used by major traditional exchanges to digital asset markets.

Recent findings suggest that valor Capital Group led the round. Adderall Capital, Keyrock and Staking Facilities also invested, alongside a small number of angel backers.

TheHUB’s first site, which is located within the Equinix TY15 data centre in Tokyo and is now live and bringing on exchanges, trading firms and validators. The tech giant will also use the money to add engineers to its team and move into further regions.

Connect Money raises $3.5m to enter Saudi Arabia and Morocco.

Connect Money, an Egypt-based FinTech offering embedded finance and white-label card services, has secured $3.5m in a pre-Series A round as it gears up to take its platform into Saudi Arabia and Morocco.

The round was led by returning backers Mohamed Farouk, Algebra Ventures and DisrupTech Ventures, according to a report from Wamda.

In a recent development, the deal blends new funding with the sale of secondary shares, giving a number of the startup’s early backers a partial exit. Connect Money has not revealed what portion of the $3.5m is new capital.

Eight by Zero lands $3m seed to fix insurance integration.

Eight by Zero, a Montréal-based InsurTech offering a universal interoperability platform for the insurance sector, has secured $3m in seed funding to expand its connectivity technology across more lines of coverage.

The round was led by Diagram, with Canada Life joining as a strategic investor.

Alongside the raise, the company, also known as 8/0, has named Munich Re Life US, part of the Munich Re Group, as its reinsurance partner. The two businesses are collaborating to tackle the difficulties group and disability insurance clients face in keeping employee data connected.

The following investor(s) were tagged in this article.

Breaking: Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1275 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • LFM3 is our upcoming generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence.
  • LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.
  • LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LFM3 is our upcoming generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:.

The payoff highlights at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Sources indicate that every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two newly introduced in-house encoders:.

Industry observers note that each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:.

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Sources indicate that reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:.

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:.

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:.

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:.

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:.

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:.

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

It has been revealed that reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:.

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:.

Industry observers note that for brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

Sources indicate that LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

We can't wait to see what you build.

Tech Report: Amazon VPC Lattice now supports CloudWatch metrics for VPC resources

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (302 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon VPC Lattice now publishes Amazon CloudWatch metrics for VPC resources.
  • Sources indicate that with these metrics, you can proactively catch connectivity problems and optimize resource capacity.
  • Recent findings suggest that cloudWatch metrics for VPC resources are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon VPC Lattice is available.

Amazon VPC Lattice now publishes Amazon CloudWatch metrics for VPC resources. Resource owners — those who share resources via VPC Lattice — and resource consumers — those who access those shared resources — can now see TCP traffic to resources such as databases, clusters, and on-premises endpoints. Resource owners get metrics for resource gateways and resource configurations. Consumers get metrics for resource endpoints, service network endpoints, and service network VPC associations. Previously, resource access logs were the primary way to see this traffic, but they required additional processing and provided limited real-time visibility. Now you can monitor your layer-4 resources directly in CloudWatch.

Sources indicate that with these metrics, you can proactively catch connectivity problems and optimize resource capacity. Capacity planning metrics — including bytes processed, latest flows, and active flows — let resource owners monitor traffic per resource gateway and per resource configuration to track load on shared resources. Reliability metrics, such as dropped packets, help you detect problems early. Resource gateways also report port allocation errors, which show when a resource gateway needs more IPv4 addresses per network interface. Consumers can monitor traffic per resource endpoint, service network endpoint, or service network VPC association. They can set CloudWatch alarms for when new flows drop to zero or dropped packets increase, catching an unreachable resource before their applications do. Both owners and consumers can break metrics down by Availability Zone to isolate zonal issues or verify connections after configuration changes.

Recent findings suggest that cloudWatch metrics for VPC resources are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon VPC Lattice is available. For the list of Regions, see the Amazon VPC Lattice FAQs.

To learn more, see CloudWatch metrics for Amazon VPC Lattice in the Amazon VPC Lattice User Guide, or visit the Amazon VPC Lattice product page.

Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2062 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that language models can do a lot.
  • Industry observers note that say a customer calls your support line.
  • In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Industry observers note that say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they remarked (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Today we're announcing two packages:.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

According to recent reports, computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's latest speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

In a recent development, it's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:.

It has been revealed that the package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:.

According to recent reports, the steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Sources indicate that parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:.

It has been revealed that qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

Recent findings suggest that to add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:.

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who noted what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:.

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

According to recent reports, we measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:.

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

It has been revealed that these numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

According to recent reports, what's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:.

In a recent development, urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

According to recent reports, emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

Industry observers note that the app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:.

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

According to recent reports, reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:.

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Industry observers note that raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Recent findings suggest that language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

AnyDecisionModel has six backends:.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

It has been revealed that like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Sources indicate that both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

Add the packages to your Package.swift:.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

According to recent reports, each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Problems and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Amazon Route 53 private hosted zones now support public DNS fallback

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (258 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Route 53 private hosted zones now support public DNS fallback.
  • According to recent reports, until now, Route 53 treated an associated private hosted zone as fully authoritative for its domain, so queries for names that weren't in the zone returned NXDOMAIN.
  • To get started, create a private Advanced Hosted Zone or upgrade an existing private hosted zone, and then turn on public DNS fallback.

Amazon Route 53 private hosted zones now support public DNS fallback. When a query for a name in your private hosted zone's domain doesn't match a record in the zone, Route 53 returns the answer from public DNS instead of a "name not found" (NXDOMAIN) error. Public DNS fallback is part of the Advanced Hosted Zones offering.

According to recent reports, until now, Route 53 treated an associated private hosted zone as fully authoritative for its domain, so queries for names that weren't in the zone returned NXDOMAIN. To resolve a few names privately, customers also had to copy every other record from their public zone into the private hosted zone and keep the two in sync. With public DNS fallback, you add only the names you need privately, and every other name resolves from your existing public DNS. For example, your private hosted zone for example.com points example.com to a private endpoint, while partner.example.com exists only in public DNS. Before, a lookup for partner.example.com returned NXDOMAIN. Now it resolves from public DNS.

To get started, create a private Advanced Hosted Zone or upgrade an existing private hosted zone, and then turn on public DNS fallback. You can use the Route 53 console, API, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or AWS CloudFormation.

Public DNS fallback is available in all AWS commercial Regions where Route 53 private hosted zones are available. To learn more, see Enabling public DNS fallback for a private hosted zone in the Route 53 Developer Guide and the Route 53 pricing page.

Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1607 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That remarked, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

In a recent development, for community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

Sources indicate that for each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

Recent findings suggest that on coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

It has been revealed that cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

According to recent reports, mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing highlighted promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Textract Core now lets AI agents extract text, tables, forms, and other data from documents through a skill, with no server to run or infrastructure to deploy.
  • You ask in natural language, and the agent returns the answers you need.
  • The skill is available at no additional charge, and standard Amazon Textract pricing applies.

Amazon Textract Core now lets AI agents extract text, tables, forms, and other data from documents through a skill, with no server to run or infrastructure to deploy. The skill guides an agent to the right Amazon Textract Core API for each document and includes a tested parser that converts the output into reading-order text and structured fields, such as answers to questions, receipt and invoice details, and identity document fields. Previously, teams that connected an agent to Amazon Textract had to build and maintain their own integration.

You ask in natural language, and the agent returns the answers you need. The skill processes multi-page PDFs and returns every page in reading order. It uses confidence scores to accept high-confidence results and flags the rest, so you can route them to your own review process. For example, you can ask an agent to turn a patient's intake form into structured data and flag unclear fields for staff review.

The skill is available at no additional charge, and standard Amazon Textract pricing applies. It is available in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon Textract is available, including: US East (Ohio), US East (N. Virginia), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Paris), Europe (Spain), and Europe (Zurich). If you use the AWS MCP server with the aws-core plugin, your agent can load the skill automatically. The skill is also published in the AWS Agent Toolkit, so agents including Kiro, Claude Code, and Cursor can use it. To learn more, see the AWS Agent Toolkit on GitHub.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS Backup now supports incremental backups of Amazon DynamoDB tables, enabling you to reduce backup storage while maintaining backup schedules as frequent as one hour.
  • Until now, AWS Backup created a full copy of your DynamoDB tables.
  • Industry observers note that AWS Backup turns on incremental backups automatically for fresh customers who protect DynamoDB.

AWS Backup now supports incremental backups of Amazon DynamoDB tables, enabling you to reduce backup storage while maintaining backup schedules as frequent as one hour.

Until now, AWS Backup created a full copy of your DynamoDB tables. With this launch, after an initial full backup, each incremental backup now captures only the data that changed, and AWS Backup takes a new full backup every 15 days. This lets you store less data and back up more often. You can restore from any recovery point in the chain, and you can schedule incremental backups anywhere from hourly to weekly frequencies. You can store incremental backups in both AWS Backup vaults and logically air-gapped vaults. Cross-Region backup copies are also incremental, further increasing your savings.

Industry observers note that AWS Backup turns on incremental backups automatically for fresh customers who protect DynamoDB. If you already back up DynamoDB with AWS Backup, you can turn on incremental backups under advanced features in AWS Backup settings, which lets you manage your backup preferences at the account and region level. You can create and manage incremental backups from the AWS Backup console, the AWS CLI, or the API.

Incremental backups for DynamoDB are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Backup protects DynamoDB. To learn more, see working with supported services in the AWS Backup Developer Guide, read the launch blog, and visit the AWS Backup product page. To get started, open the AWS Backup console.

#16620. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1321 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
  • Recent findings suggest that today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research.
  • The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Recent findings suggest that today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Sources indicate that participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

According to recent reports, the U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

In a recent development, project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

It has been revealed that the demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

In a recent development, the pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many fresh science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Sources indicate that figure 1. Newly introduced public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

Industry observers note that when organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

Sources indicate that this is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an crucial first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

According to recent reports, to explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Industry observers note that participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

It has been revealed that teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

According to recent reports, the CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be revealed through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

Industry observers note that we also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

Previously, organizations lacked a standardized way to distinguish verified bots from malicious traffic. Now, bots can prove domain ownership through WebBotAuth, and you can integrate this verification with AWS WAF Bot Control to write rules that combine verification status and bot identity.

Recent findings suggest that this new capability gives content providers and application developers fine-grained control over which bots can access your resources. You can enhance security and improve traffic management by distinguishing legitimate bots from malicious actors. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding fresh expertise on a single endpoint.

Sources indicate that granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

It has been revealed that while we are excited about these fresh features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this revision. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the latest multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

Recent findings suggest that AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing (formerly AWS Security Agent) now lets you estimate task hours before running a penetration test, so developers and security teams can see how many billable task hours a test is likely to need and choose a maximum task-hours limit with confidence. Continuum for Penetration Testing runs on-demand, AI-driven penetration tests against your web applications and APIs. Previously, the only way to know how long a test would take was to run it, making it difficult to strategy budgets and set appropriate usage limits.

According to recent reports, with task-hour estimates, you open a penetration test, choose the Pentest cost estimate tab, and request an estimate. AWS Continuum runs a short preliminary analysis of your application's scope. It then draws on expertise from past penetration tests to estimate the task hours needed and shows the task hours that most similar applications finish within, and the higher range a few applications require. Requesting an estimate is free, and the estimate is a guide, not a quote or a limit. Actual task hours can be higher or lower, and only the maximum task-hours limit caps usage.

Task-hour estimates are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing is available.

To learn more, see the documentation. To get started, visit the AWS Continuum product page.
